idiom_name: read-only List over a private MutableList
implementation_notes: Kotlin encodes the distinction in the stdlib as two interfaces: keep `private val _courses = mutableListOf<Course>()` and publish `val courses: List<Course> get() = _courses` - `List` has no add/remove/set, so the compiler rejects mutation at the call site. The documentation is explicit that this restricts mutability through the reference only: with a `List` reference to a `MutableList` you get compile errors on `referenceList.add(4)` while `sourceList.add(4)` still changes what the reference sees; `toList()` produces a real snapshot (a shallow copy) when callers must not observe later changes. Membership changes go through addCourse/removeCourse, which own validation and derived state.
pitfalls: `List` over a `MutableList` is a live view, not a snapshot: readers observe later additions - use `toList()` where isolation is required, and say which one the property returns.
Casting the read-only reference (`courses as MutableList`) or widening the property type to `MutableList` reopens mutation; the declared property type is the contract.
Java interop sees `java.util.List`, which has mutators; a Java-facing API must hand out `toList()` copies or an immutable collection.
The mutable field is still reachable inside the class, so any internal code path that adds without updating derived state (counts, caches) breaks the invariant the pattern is supposed to protect.
